patient.name: Sandra Whitfield
patient.setting: GP surgery, then acute oncology and the oncology ward
patient.complaint: Mid-back pain for 5 weeks, worse at night, and weight loss
background: Breast cancer 6 years ago: wide local excision, radiotherapy, now on letrozole

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a new symptom in a patient with a cancer history (back pain, headache, hepatomegaly), or 'Which primary is most likely?' from the pattern of spread (cannonball lungs = renal, sclerotic bone = prostate).

points: 5 weeks of mid-back pain, **worse at night**, waking her.
No trauma, no leg weakness, bladder and bowels normal.

steps.lead: Sandra's **known primary** is the biggest risk factor; her old smoking history adds a little.

steps.q: What should you assume Sandra's new back pain is until proven otherwise?
steps.r: A new symptom in someone with a cancer history is **metastasis until proven otherwise**; night pain makes **spinal metastasis** likely.

steps.lead: Sandra has **B symptoms**, fatigue and night-time bone pain: the systemic picture of spread.

points: Liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin.
Right thigh aches when she walks.
Legs: normal power, sensation and reflexes.

visual.title: Where Sandra's liver is felt
visual.caption: Smooth, firm, slightly irregular hepatomegaly: think liver metastases.

steps.lead: Bone is the commonest place to find metastases and the **spine** the commonest bone, exactly where Sandra hurts.
Her big liver points to **liver metastases**. A new headache with vomiting would mean brain spread and **raised ICP**.
Sandra's breast cancer has spread through the blood (**haematogenous**) to bone and liver; it also commonly spreads via lymphatics.

steps.text: Do not blame **osteoporosis** because she is on letrozole. Night pain, weight loss and a cancer history mean **metastasis** until imaging says otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': MRI spine for new back pain in a cancer patient, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging, and imaging plus biopsy to confirm the origin.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line imaging for Sandra's back pain?
o: Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine
steps.r: New back pain in a cancer patient needs an **MRI spine**. A plain X-ray can miss early spinal metastases.

steps.lead: Sandra has an **MRI spine** for her back, **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis** to stage, and bloods including **calcium**.

steps.title: Sandra's bloods
steps.text: High **calcium** suggests bone involvement; high ALP and GGT fit **liver** and bone deposits.

visual.title: Adjusted calcium
visual.label: Sandra 2.86
visual.caption: Raised calcium in a cancer patient: think bone metastases.

points: MRI spine: deposit in **T8** vertebral body; cord not compressed.
CT: several **liver** lesions; **lytic** lesion in the right femur.
No lung or brain lesions seen.

steps.lead: Imaging found the deposits; an image-guided **liver biopsy** confirms they are breast cancer, not a new primary.

steps.title: Work-up of suspected metastases
nodes: New symptom in a cancer patient
steps.caption: Imaging finds it; biopsy proves where it came from.

steps.text: Imaging alone does not prove origin. A liver lesion in a breast cancer survivor could be a **new primary**: the gold standard is **imaging plus biopsy**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': oncology MDT systemic therapy, bisphosphonates for bone metastases, steroids plus radiotherapy for brain metastases, prophylactic fixation if Mirels ≥9, and palliative care.

steps.lead: Sandra's case goes to the **oncology MDT**: her biopsy is hormone-receptor positive, so she starts **systemic** targeted and endocrine therapy.
For her bones Sandra gets a **bisphosphonate**; palliative care helps with pain and fatigue from the start.

points: The femoral lesion is lytic, in the **peritrochanteric** region.

visual.title: Mirels score: right femur
visual.label: Sandra 11
visual.caption: Site 3 (peritrochanteric) + pain 3 (functional) + lytic 3 + size 2 (one third to two thirds of the cortex) = 11.

steps.q: Sandra's Mirels score is 11. What should happen to her femur?
o: Wait for a fracture, then fix
steps.r: **Mirels ≥9** (or >50% cortical destruction with weight-bearing pain) means **prophylactic surgery** before it fractures.

steps.lead: Sandra's femur is pinned with an intramedullary nail before it breaks, followed by radiotherapy.
Her score of 11 uses the **Mirels** system: site, pain, lesion type and size, each scored 1 to 3.

points: 4 months later: morning **headaches** and **vomiting** for a week.

steps.lead: Headache plus vomiting in Sandra means **brain metastases with raised ICP**: urgent same-day assessment and imaging.

steps.title: Brain metastases with raised ICP
steps.caption: Steroids work in hours on the oedema around the deposits.

steps.text: Match the treatment to the site: **bisphosphonates** for bone, **steroids + radiotherapy** for brain, **systemic therapy** via the MDT for the disease, **palliative care** throughout.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the route of spread (haematogenous, lymphatic, transcoelomic), why prostate gives sclerotic lesions, or why bone metastases raise calcium.

steps.lead: Sandra's breast cancer cells broke into blood vessels, survived the circulation and settled in her spine and liver.

steps.title: The metastatic cascade
nodes: Arrest and extravasation at a distant site

steps.lead: Haematogenous spread favours well-supplied organs. For a bowel cancer, the **portal vein** carries cells straight to the liver.
Sandra's femur lesion is **lytic**: osteoclasts eat the bone and weaken it. Prostate cancer would make **sclerotic** bone instead.

steps.q: Which mechanism best explains Sandra's raised calcium?
steps.r: Lytic deposits activate **osteoclasts** and release calcium; PTHrP-like activity can add to it. Osteoblastic (prostate) lesions build bone.

steps.lead: Sandra's calcium of 2.86 comes from **osteolysis** at her bone deposits, possibly helped by PTHrP-like activity.
Sandra's spread needed blood vessels. **Ovarian** cancer can simply shed into the peritoneal cavity and implant there.

mcq.q: Which is the most common mechanism of metastatic spread?
Which is the most common site of bone metastases?
mcq.r: The **spine**: new back pain in a cancer patient is spinal metastasis until proven otherwise.

mcq.q: Cannonball metastases in the lungs classically come from which primary?
Which is the most common site of colorectal cancer metastasis?
Which is first-line imaging for new back pain in a patient with cancer?
Which confirms metastatic disease and its origin?
mcq.r: **Imaging plus biopsy** is the gold standard.

mcq.q: Which Mirels score indicates prophylactic orthopaedic fixation?
mcq.r: **Mirels ≥9**, or a lytic lesion involving >50% of the cortex with weight-bearing pain.

mcq.q: Which drug class is used long-term for bone metastases?
How are brain metastases with oedema managed?
mcq.r: **Steroids** reduce the oedema; **radiotherapy** treats the deposits.

mcq.q: Why does prostate cancer cause sclerotic bone lesions?
mcq.r: Prostate cancer stimulates **osteoblastic** activity; most others are lytic via osteoclasts.

prompts.q: What is metastatic disease, and how does it usually present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: new symptom + cancer history = metastasis until proven otherwise.

points.p: Spread from a primary tumour to distant sites forming secondary tumours
points.why: Risk factors: known primary, smoking, genetic predisposition.

points.p: B symptoms: weight loss, night sweats, fever; fatigue
points.why: Systemic symptoms of a high tumour burden.

points.p: Pain, bone tenderness, hepatomegaly, neurological deficit
points.why: Signs depend on which organ is involved.

points.p: New back pain in a cancer patient = spinal metastasis until proven otherwise
points.why: Night pain is the red flag.

prompts.q: How do bone, liver, lung and brain metastases each present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the symptom names the organ.

points.p: Bone: pain worse at night, pathological fractures; spine commonest
points.why: Bone is the most common metastatic site in the notes.

points.p: Liver: hepatomegaly, abnormal LFTs, weight loss
Lung: breathlessness and cough
Brain: headache, seizures, focal deficit; headache + vomiting = raised ICP

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the pattern of spread points to the primary.

points.p: Prostate: bone, osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions
points.why: The commonest male cancer to spread to bone.

points.p: Breast: lung, liver, brain, bone
Colorectal: liver
Renal cell carcinoma: cannonball lung metastases
Lung cancer also commonly spreads to bone

prompts.q: Name the four routes of metastatic spread, with an example of each.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ovary in the peritoneum = transcoelomic.

points.p: Haematogenous: most common, e.g. to brain and spine
Lymphatic: common in breast cancer
Transcoelomic: across body cavities, e.g. ovarian carcinoma, mesothelioma
Canalicular: along bile ducts, airways, urinary tract, subarachnoid space

prompts.q: How do you investigate suspected metastatic disease, and what confirms it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: MRI for the spine, CT for staging, biopsy for proof.

points.p: MRI spine first-line for new back pain; MRI for suspected CNS disease
points.why: Plain X-rays miss early spinal deposits.

points.p: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging
Bloods: FBC, LFTs, calcium (raised calcium suggests bone involvement)
points.why: Calcium and ALP for bone; LFTs for liver.

points.p: Imaging plus biopsy is gold standard: confirms diagnosis and origin
points.why: A new primary must be excluded.

prompts.q: What are the principles of managing metastatic disease?

points.p: Systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy) via the oncology MDT
Bisphosphonates for bone metastases
points.why: Reduce bone pain, fractures and hypercalcaemia.

points.p: Brain metastases: steroids to reduce oedema, with radiotherapy
Palliative care (symptom control) is most important in many
points.why: Most metastatic disease is not curable.

prompts.q: When is prophylactic orthopaedic surgery indicated for a bone metastasis, and what is urgent in a cancer patient with headache?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the number 9 and the 50% cortex rule.

points.p: Mirels score of 9 or more
points.why: Scores site, pain, lesion type and size.

points.p: Large lytic lesion involving >50% of the cortex with weight-bearing pain
Headache and vomiting = brain metastases with raised ICP: urgent assessment

prompts.q: Describe the steps of the metastatic cascade, and why haematogenous spread favours certain organs.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: invade, intravasate, survive, extravasate, grow.

points.p: Local invasion
Intravasation into vessels or lymphatics; survive in circulation
Arrest, extravasation and proliferation at a distant site
First capillary bed reached, e.g. portal vein takes GI cancers to the liver
points.why: Lung, liver, brain and bone are highly vascular.

prompts.q: Why are some bone metastases sclerotic and others lytic, and why do they raise calcium?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: prostate builds bone; most others eat it.

points.p: Prostate stimulates osteoblasts: sclerotic lesions
points.why: Raised ALP with normal calcium is common.

points.p: Lung, renal, thyroid (breast mixed) are lytic via osteoclast activation
Osteolysis releases calcium into the blood
PTHrP-like activity adds to hypercalcaemia

glossary.metastasis: A secondary tumour formed when cancer cells spread from the primary to a distant site.
glossary.primary tumour: The original cancer from which metastases come.
glossary.B symptoms: Weight loss, night sweats and fever, reflecting a high tumour burden.
glossary.haematogenous: Spread through the bloodstream; the most common route of metastasis.
glossary.lymphatic spread: Spread through lymph vessels to lymph nodes, common in breast cancer.
glossary.transcoelomic: Spread across a body cavity such as the peritoneum or pleura, e.g. ovarian cancer.
glossary.canalicular: Spread along natural channels such as bile ducts, airways or the urinary tract.
glossary.intravasation: Tumour cells breaking into blood or lymphatic vessels.
glossary.extravasation: Tumour cells leaving a vessel to enter tissue at a distant site.
glossary.cannonball metastases: Multiple large round lung metastases, classically from renal cell carcinoma.
glossary.renal cell carcinoma: The commonest kidney cancer; classically gives cannonball lung metastases.
glossary.osteoblastic: Bone-forming; prostate cancer metastases stimulate osteoblasts and make sclerotic lesions.
glossary.osteolytic: Bone-destroying, via osteoclast activation; most bone metastases are lytic.
glossary.sclerotic: Dense, white-looking bone lesions on X-ray from extra bone formation.
glossary.lytic: Holes in bone on imaging where it has been destroyed.
glossary.osteoclast: Cell that breaks down bone, activated by lytic metastases.
glossary.osteoblast: Cell that builds bone, stimulated by prostate cancer metastases.
glossary.pathological fracture: A fracture through bone weakened by disease, often after trivial force.
glossary.Mirels score: Score of site, pain, lesion type and size (each 1 to 3); 9 or more means prophylactic fixation.
glossary.prophylactic fixation: Surgically stabilising a bone before it fractures.
glossary.LFTs: Liver function tests: bilirubin, ALT, ALP, GGT and albumin.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase; raised by bone metastases and liver or biliary disease.
glossary.GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase; a liver enzyme that confirms a liver source for raised ALP.
glossary.hypercalcaemia of malignancy: High calcium from cancer, via bone destruction or PTHrP.
glossary.PTHrP: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide; mimics PTH and raises calcium.
glossary.ICP: Intracranial pressure; raised by brain metastases and their oedema.
glossary.raised ICP: High pressure in the skull: headache worse in the morning, vomiting, papilloedema.
glossary.MDT: Multidisciplinary team: oncologists, surgeons, radiologists and others planning care together.
glossary.bisphosphonates: Drugs that inhibit osteoclasts, used for bone metastases (e.g. zoledronic acid).
glossary.zoledronic acid: Intravenous bisphosphonate used for bone metastases and hypercalcaemia.
glossary.dexamethasone: Potent steroid used to reduce oedema around brain metastases.
glossary.radiotherapy: Treatment with ionising radiation to shrink tumours or relieve pain.
glossary.palliative care: Care focused on symptom control and quality of life when cure is not possible.
glossary.letrozole: Aromatase inhibitor used after breast cancer; causes bone loss.
glossary.omental cake: Thickened omentum infiltrated by tumour, typical of ovarian cancer spread.
glossary.portal vein: Vein carrying blood from the gut to the liver, explaining liver metastases from bowel cancer.
glossary.peritrochanteric: Around the trochanters of the upper femur; the highest-risk Mirels site.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with small cell lung cancer diagnosed 3 months ago has a 1 week history of headaches that are worst on waking, with vomiting. Today he noticed weakness of his right hand. His pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 158/92 mmHg. He has mild right-sided weakness.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a new neurological problem in a cancer patient.

clues: pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 158/92 mmHg
steps.x: Raised ICP pattern (morning headache, vomiting, slowish pulse, high BP) plus a **focal** deficit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brain metastases** with raised ICP.

elim: Hypercalcaemia causes confusion and vomiting but not focal weakness.
A new migraine at 66 with focal weakness in a cancer patient is not migraine.
Cerebellar degeneration gives ataxia, not headache and hemiparesis.
SAH is a sudden thunderclap headache, not a week of morning headaches.

steps.x: **A. Brain metastases.** Rule: cancer + headache + vomiting + focal sign = brain metastases.

technique.stem: A 59 year old woman had a right hemicolectomy for colon cancer 2 years ago. At follow-up she reports 3 months of fatigue and 6 kg weight loss. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Her liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation: first-line staging for suspected metastatic disease.
Bowel cancer history, systemic symptoms, hepatomegaly, rising CEA and cholestatic LFTs: **liver metastases**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stage with **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis**.

elim: No bone pain; a bone scan does not stage the liver.
Colonoscopy looks for local recurrence, not distant spread.
MRI spine is for new back pain.
PET is a later problem-solving test, not first-line staging.

steps.x: **C. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis.** Rule: suspected metastases = CT CAP first; biopsy confirms.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man with prostate cancer has new bone metastases in his spine and pelvis on bone scan. His pain is controlled with paracetamol and codeine. He is mobile with no neurological signs. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. The oncology team has started androgen deprivation therapy.
technique.q: Which additional long-term treatment is most appropriate for his bone metastases?

steps.x: Long-term, site-specific treatment for bone metastases.

clues: new bone metastases in his spine and pelvis
steps.x: Stable bone disease, no fracture risk features, no cord compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bisphosphonate** to protect the bones.

elim: Calcium gluconate treats hyperkalaemia or hypocalcaemia.
Steroids are for brain metastases with oedema.
Fixation needs Mirels ≥9 or >50% cortical loss with pain; none described.
Thiazides raise calcium; they do not treat bone metastases.

steps.x: **A. Bisphosphonate.** Rule: bone metastases = bisphosphonate, alongside MDT systemic therapy.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man had an anterior resection for rectal cancer 18 months ago. CT now shows multiple lesions in the liver but none in the lungs or bones. His pulse rate is 76 bpm. Liver biopsy shows adenocarcinoma of colorectal origin.
technique.q: Which is the most likely route by which the tumour reached his liver?
o: Canalicular spread along the bile ducts

steps.x: A route-of-spread question.

clues: none in the lungs or bones
steps.x: Bowel primary, liver-only deposits: the liver is the **first capillary bed** after the gut.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haematogenous spread via the portal vein.**

elim: Canalicular spread runs along ducts from a biliary primary, not from the rectum.
The rectum is not next to the liver.
Lymphatic spread goes to nodes, not to multiple liver deposits.
Transcoelomic spread seeds the peritoneal surface, as in ovarian cancer.

steps.x: **D. Portal venous spread.** Rule: GI cancer → portal vein → liver.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with prostate cancer treated 3 years ago has a 6 week history of lower back pain that wakes him at night. He has lost 4 kg. There is no history of trauma. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. He is tender over L2. Leg power, sensation and reflexes are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: New night back pain and weight loss in a man with prostate cancer, with a raised ALP, is a spinal metastasis until proven otherwise. Osteomyelitis would give fever and a high CRP.

steps.x: Diagnosis of new back pain: check for a cancer history first.
Night pain, weight loss, raised ALP (osteoblastic lesions), cancer history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Spinal metastasis.**

elim: Night pain and weight loss are red flags against mechanical pain.
Myeloma gives lytic lesions, high calcium and a normal ALP.
Osteoporotic collapse is sudden after minor strain; ALP is normal.
No fever and a near-normal CRP make infection unlikely.

steps.x: **D. Spinal metastasis.** Rule: cancer history + new back pain = metastasis until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a 2 month history of breathlessness, cough and 8 kg weight loss. He has had two episodes of painless visible haematuria and a left flank mass is palpable. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 148/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple large, round, well-defined lesions in both lungs.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Multiple round 'cannonball' lung lesions with haematuria, a flank mass and polycythaemia are metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Miliary TB gives tiny millet-seed nodules.

steps.x: Diagnosis: link the chest film to the rest of the history.
Haematuria + flank mass + raised haemoglobin (EPO) + **cannonball** lung lesions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Renal cell carcinoma** with lung metastases.

elim: Miliary TB shows innumerable tiny nodules, not large round masses.
A lung primary would not explain haematuria and a flank mass.
Sarcoid gives bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
Septic emboli come with fever and cavitating nodules, e.g. in IV drug users.

steps.x: **A. Metastatic renal cell carcinoma.** Rule: cannonball metastases = renal cell carcinoma.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman treated for ovarian carcinoma 1 year ago has a 4 week history of abdominal swelling, early satiety and weight loss. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. There is shifting dullness. CT abdomen shows ascites, omental thickening and multiple nodules on the peritoneal surfaces. The liver parenchyma is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Ascites with omental cake and peritoneal nodules after ovarian carcinoma is transcoelomic spread to the peritoneum. Cirrhosis would show an abnormal liver and no peritoneal nodules.

steps.x: Diagnosis of ascites in a cancer patient.

clues: omental thickening and multiple nodules on the peritoneal surfaces
steps.x: Ovarian primary, peritoneal deposits, normal liver.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Peritoneal metastases** by transcoelomic spread.

elim: Cirrhosis shows a shrunken nodular liver; this liver is normal.
Nephrotic syndrome causes generalised oedema and proteinuria, not peritoneal nodules.
Right heart failure gives raised JVP and leg oedema.
TB peritonitis is possible but the ovarian history makes metastasis far likelier.

steps.x: **C. Peritoneal metastases.** Rule: ovary + peritoneal nodules = transcoelomic spread.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman had breast cancer treated 4 years ago. She has 2 months of fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort and 5 kg weight loss. She drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. She has a firm, irregular liver edge 5 cm below the costal margin.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Firm, irregular hepatomegaly with a cholestatic rise (ALP, GGT), weight loss and a breast cancer history are liver metastases. Hepatitis A gives a much higher ALT.

steps.x: Diagnosis: new liver signs in a cancer survivor.
Cancer history, weight loss, irregular **hepatomegaly**, raised ALP and GGT, minimal alcohol.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Liver metastases.**

elim: She drinks only 4 units a week; alcoholic hepatitis needs heavy drinking.
Biliary colic causes episodic pain, not irregular hepatomegaly and weight loss.
Hepatitis A gives ALT in the thousands and jaundice.
PBC presents with itch and fatigue in middle-aged women, without irregular hepatomegaly.

steps.x: **D. Liver metastases.** Rule: cancer history + irregular liver + abnormal LFTs = liver metastases.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has a 3 month history of pain in his pelvis and lower back. He has had poor urinary stream and nocturia for 2 years. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. X-rays show multiple dense, sclerotic lesions in the pelvis and lumbar vertebrae.
practice.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
practice.e: Sclerotic (osteoblastic) bone metastases in an older man with urinary symptoms point to prostate cancer, the commonest male cancer to spread to bone. Lung, renal and thyroid metastases are lytic.

steps.x: A primary-site question: use the type of bone lesion.
**Sclerotic** lesions, high ALP, normal calcium, prostatic symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prostate.**

elim: Bladder cancer gives haematuria and rarely sclerotic bone deposits.
Lung metastases to bone are lytic.
Renal metastases are lytic.
Thyroid metastases are lytic.

steps.x: **C. Prostate.** Rule: sclerotic bone metastases in a man = prostate.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer felt a sudden severe pain in her left thigh while turning in bed and cannot weight-bear. She had 2 months of aching in the thigh, worse at night. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. X-ray shows a transverse fracture through a lytic lesion in the proximal femoral shaft.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A fracture with trivial force through a lytic lesion in a woman with metastatic breast cancer, after weeks of night pain, is a pathological fracture through a metastasis. Osteoporotic fractures do not occur through a lytic lesion.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a fracture: look at the force and the bone.
Trivial force, prior night pain, **lytic** lesion, cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pathological fracture** through a bone metastasis.

elim: Osteomalacia gives diffuse bone pain and Looser zones, not a lytic lesion.
Osteoporosis thins bone evenly; it does not cause a focal lytic lesion.
Paget's gives thickened, expanded bone with mixed lysis and sclerosis.
Stress fractures follow repetitive loading in active people.

steps.x: **D. Pathological fracture.** Rule: trivial force + lytic lesion + cancer = pathological fracture.

practice.stem: A 65 year old woman with lung cancer diagnosed 6 months ago has a 2 week history of thoracic back pain, worse lying down and at night. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. She is tender over T6. Leg power and sensation are normal and she is passing urine normally.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine
practice.e: New back pain in a patient with cancer needs MRI spine first-line to look for spinal metastasis. A plain X-ray can miss early deposits, and a bone scan does not show the spinal canal.

steps.x: Initial investigation for back pain in a cancer patient.

clues: worse lying down and at night
steps.x: Cancer + new night back pain: **spinal metastasis** until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI spine.**

elim: A bone scan finds deposits but not their effect on the cord.
CT shows bone but not the cord or soft tissue as well as MRI.
PET is for staging, not first-line for back pain.
X-rays miss early metastases.

steps.x: **C. MRI spine.** Rule: new back pain + cancer = MRI spine.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has 3 months of weight loss and fatigue. He has no known cancer. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows multiple lesions in the liver typical of metastases, but no obvious primary tumour. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis and its origin?
practice.e: Imaging plus biopsy is the gold standard: histology confirms metastasis and shows the tumour of origin. More imaging or tumour markers cannot prove the origin.

steps.x: 'Confirm and origin' means tissue.

clues: multiple lesions in the liver typical of metastases
steps.x: Metastases of unknown primary: histology is needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Biopsy** of a liver lesion.

elim: Ultrasound adds no tissue and less detail than CT.
MRI characterises lesions but gives no histology.
PET-CT may find a primary but does not prove origin.
Tumour markers are supportive, not diagnostic.

steps.x: **A. Liver biopsy.** Rule: imaging finds metastases; biopsy proves them.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with metastatic lung cancer has a 5 day history of worsening morning headache and vomiting. She has a mild left hemiparesis. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm, BP 156/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and GCS 15. MRI brain shows two enhancing lesions with extensive surrounding oedema.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Brain metastases with oedema causing raised ICP are treated urgently with steroids (dexamethasone) to reduce oedema, followed by radiotherapy. Lumbar puncture is dangerous with raised ICP.

steps.x: Initial management of an oncological emergency.
Brain metastases with **oedema** and raised ICP, but conscious and stable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Steroids** (dexamethasone), then radiotherapy.

elim: Bisphosphonates are for bone metastases.
LP with raised ICP and mass lesions risks coning.
Mannitol and intubation are for impending herniation; her GCS is 15.
She has not had a seizure, and an anticonvulsant does not treat the oedema.

steps.x: **B. Dexamethasone.** Rule: brain metastases with oedema = steroids + radiotherapy.

practice.stem: An 84 year old man has widespread metastatic pancreatic cancer in his liver and lungs. He spends most of the day in bed and is breathless and in pain. He has said he does not want further chemotherapy and wishes to stay at home. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: In advanced incurable metastatic disease, palliative care for symptom control is the most important step, respecting his wish to stay at home and decline chemotherapy.

steps.x: Next step in advanced disease: what matters most to this patient?

clues: spends most of the day in bed
steps.x: Poor performance status, symptoms, clear wishes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Specialist palliative care** for symptom control.

elim: He has declined chemotherapy and is too frail.
Resection is not curative with lung metastases.
No bone lesion is described.
No brain metastases are described.

steps.x: **D. Palliative care.** Rule: advanced incurable disease = symptom control first.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has pain in her right hip when walking. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the peritrochanteric region of the right femur destroying more than half the cortical thickness. Her Mirels score is 11.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the femoral lesion?
practice.e: A Mirels score of 9 or more, or a lytic lesion over 50% of the cortex with weight-bearing pain, needs prophylactic fixation before it fractures, usually followed by radiotherapy.

steps.x: Management of a bone lesion: is fracture risk high?

practice.stem: A 69 year old man with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer has confusion, constipation and thirst. Bone scan shows multiple lytic deposits in the ribs and pelvis. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his raised calcium?
o: Increased intestinal calcium absorption from vitamin D
Osteolysis by activated osteoclasts at bone deposits
Reduced renal calcium excretion from thiazides
practice.e: Lytic bone metastases activate osteoclasts and release calcium (with PTHrP-like activity adding to it), and native PTH is suppressed. Osteoblast stimulation is the prostate pattern and builds bone.

steps.x: A mechanism question about calcium in metastatic disease.
Symptomatic hypercalcaemia, **lytic** deposits, PTH suppressed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osteolysis** by osteoclasts releasing calcium.

elim: Vitamin D excess is granulomatous (sarcoid), not lytic deposits.
Osteoblast stimulation makes sclerotic lesions, as in prostate cancer.
PTH is suppressed, so not an adenoma.
No thiazide is mentioned.

steps.x: **C. Osteolysis.** Rule: lytic metastases + high calcium + low PTH = osteolysis (plus PTHrP).
